screens.title: Applying LSP: Practical Examples and Refactoring
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how to spot real Liskov Substitution Principle violations in working code, and how to refactor them so clients never need to distinguish concrete subtypes. We’ll move from concrete indicators — methods that throw or silently do nothing — to practical fixes like extracting narrower interfaces and preferring composition. You will see real examples such as discount calculators, printable documents, and report generators. For each example we will name the violating behavior, show a refactoring pattern, and explain why the refactor restores substitutability. This matters because breaking LSP produces brittle code: client code begins to branch on types, to check instances, or to catch unexpected exceptions. Those symptoms hide design debt and increase maintenance cost. By following the checks and refactor patterns you’ll be able to design class hierarchies that are predictable, easier to test, and safer to extend. Think about the last time you saw an instanceof check in production: by the end of this chapter you’ll be able to ask the right questions and suggest a concrete refactor.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will analyze existing code and detect LSP violations that show up as runtime surprises or client-side branching. You will practice concrete refactorings such as extracting narrower interfaces, introducing new abstractions, and applying composition to avoid behavioral mismatch. You will learn to weigh trade-offs encountered during real-world refactors, such as added indirection versus clearer contracts, and you will design new class hierarchies that preserve substitutability from the start. These skills matter because they reduce debugging time, avoid fragile client code, and improve testability and extensibility. For example, after learning the extract-interface technique you will be able to replace a single base class method that cannot be implemented by all subtypes with two smaller interfaces, enabling clients to depend only on the behavior they need. Think of these objectives as a practical checklist: identify, refactor, evaluate, and design. Each objective pairs a practical skill with why it matters in production systems.

screens.title: What an LSP violation looks like in real code
screens.narratorSegment: An LSP violation happens when a subtype cannot stand in for its base type without surprising clients. In practice this shows up as a handful of clear symptoms. One is methods that throw specific exceptions when a client expects general behavior. Another is methods that silently do nothing — for example a subclass that overrides a base method with an empty implementation; clients then receive no effect where one was expected. A third symptom is client code that performs type checks or branches based on subclass type instead of relying on polymorphism. Those branches are a sign the subclass does not preserve the base contract. Consider a logging class: if a subclass requires extra initialization and throws if it’s not provided, client calls that assume a simple log call will break. A misconception is to think that different return values alone imply violation — different results are acceptable if they still meet the base method’s postconditions. To be an LSP violation we need changed preconditions (the subtype requires more), changed postconditions (the subtype fails to meet promised results), or unexpected side effects. Example: a discount calculator that throws when not a first-time customer changes the precondition. The takeaway is simple: when a client must reason about concrete types or handle unexpected exceptions from an override, the design needs a narrower abstraction or a different composition. How might you test for substitutability in your codebase?

keyIdea.title: Detection checklist
keyIdea.text: Look for thrown errors, no-op overrides, and client-side instanceof checks; any of these can signal an LSP violation.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › LSP Violations
What an LSP violation looks like
Symptoms and a quick detection checklist
Common Symptoms
  • Overrides that throw unexpected exceptions or require extra state.
  • Methods that become no-ops in subclasses while clients expect action.
  • Client code checking concrete types to decide behavior.
Misconception Check
Different outputs do not automatically mean violation. The important question is whether outputs still satisfy the base contract's postconditions and side effects.
Example Scenario
A discount class that throws unless a customer is first-time has introduced a new precondition; client code expecting any discount object will be surprised.
Quick Substitutability Test
  1. Replace a base instance with a subtype in tests.
  2. Run all clients that depend on the base API.
  3. Observe unexpected exceptions, changed side effects, or failing assertions.
Common Mistake
Forcing inheritance for code reuse rather than behavioral correctness often leads to these violations.

screens.title: Indicators and counter-examples
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the difference between acceptable behavioral difference and an LSP violation is central to good design. A valid subtype can return different concrete values as long as it honors the base contract. For instance, two discount calculators that both return a numeric discount are substitutable even if the formulas differ. Contrast this with a subtype that returns zero for most inputs or throws when certain conditions are not met: that alters the expected postcondition or adds a new precondition. A helpful concrete example contrasts a StandardDiscountCalculator and a FirstTimeCustomerDiscountCalculator. The standard implementation applies a percent to the total and always returns a numeric discount. The first-time implementation, if written to throw for repeat customers, changes the contract and violates LSP. A misconception is to treat any conditional logic inside a subtype as a violation. Conditional behavior is fine if the method still meets all preconditions and postconditions the base type promises. The practical test is simple: can client code call the base method on the subtype in the same way and expect the same kinds of results and side effects? If not, refactor by splitting the abstraction or using composition. Which refactor will preserve behavior without adding client complexity?

keyIdea.text: Different implementations are allowed; changing required inputs or expected outputs is not.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Indicators
Preserving behavior vs violating it
Concrete contrast to sharpen your design choices
Valid Subtype: StandardDiscountCalculator
Returns a numeric discount for any input and does not add new requirements. Clients always receive a number and can proceed reliably.
Why it’s safe
  • Preconditions unchanged — any total amount is accepted.
  • Postconditions met — a numeric discount is returned.
Violating Subtype: FirstTimeCustomerDiscountCalculator
If it throws for repeat customers or returns zero unexpectedly, it either adds a precondition or alters the postcondition and will surprise clients.
Misconception
Returning zero is only acceptable if the base contract allows zero. Otherwise it breaks expectations.
Design response
If a behavior is conditional to a customer state, extract a new abstraction or require the state via an interface. That way clients depending on unconditional discount logic are not broken.

screens.title: Introduce narrower abstractions
screens.narratorSegment: A primary refactor for LSP problems is to extract a narrower abstraction that captures the true contract. When the base class exposes methods not meaningful for every subtype, the base is too broad. The fix is to split responsibilities: define smaller interfaces or abstract classes describing the capability precisely. For example, instead of a generic Vehicle that includes a refuel method, create a Refuelable interface. Car implements Refuelable, Bicycle does not. Client code that needs to refuel depends on Refuelable, not Vehicle. This prevents Bicycle being passed where refueling is expected. In practice perform the refactor in three steps: first, identify methods that cause violations; second, extract an interface with those methods and update types; third, migrate subclasses to implement the new interface only if they satisfy the contract. A common pitfall is extracting too many tiny interfaces without clear purpose; balance specificity and usability. Concrete scenario: the Document class with a print method that SecureDocument cannot implement without extra state. Extract a Printable interface with get_printable_content and have both simple and secure documents implement it. The client then prints any Printable without caring about encryption. Ask yourself: which methods in my base class are actually optional for some subclasses?

keyIdea.title: Refactor pattern
keyIdea.text: Extract a smaller interface for methods that are not universally implementable, then update clients to depend on the new interface.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Extract Interface
Introduce narrower abstractions
A step-by-step process to salvage substitutability
Three-step refactor
  1. Detect methods that cause client branching or exceptions.
  2. Extract a focused interface capturing only required operations.
  3. Have only suitable subclasses implement the interface; update clients to depend on it.
Example: move from Document.print_document which SecureDocument cannot implement cleanly, to a Printable interface exposing get_printable_content. Clients call print_any_document on Printable and never worry about encryption details.
Visual mnemonic
Think of extracting an interface as carving a smaller, safer contract out of a larger one so clients depend only on what they need.
Key Takeaway

Extracting narrow interfaces lets clients rely on guaranteed behavior and prevents subclasses from inheriting methods they cannot satisfy.

screens.title: Use composition when 'is-a' fails
screens.narratorSegment: Composition is the alternative when a class needs certain behavior but does not truly 'is-a' the base type. Instead of inheriting and being forced to implement or disable methods, the class can hold an instance that provides the required functionality and delegate to it. That avoids adding preconditions or surprising side effects. A concrete example is a Logger that has FileLogger and DatabaseLogger as subclasses. If you then create an EmailLogger that primarily sends email but also logs, composition is a natural fit: EmailLogger should contain a Logger and an EmailSender rather than inherit from Logger and extend its responsibilities. This keeps Logger's contract intact and lets EmailLogger delegate only the parts it needs. A misconception is believing composition always adds more code; while it can introduce small forwarding methods, it preserves behavior and reduces the chance of violating contracts. Composition also makes testing simpler: you can inject a mock component rather than stub an inherited method. Ask yourself: does my subclass change the meaning of a base method? If yes, consider composition and delegation instead of inheritance. Use composition when 'is-a' fails means when behavior doesn't semantically match an 'is-a' relationship, prefer 'has-a' with delegation to preserve contracts and simplify testing.. In practical terms, delegate behavior instead of forcing incorrect inheritance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Composition
Use composition when 'is-a' fails
Delegate capabilities to preserve base contracts and reduce surprises.
When to choose composition
  • Your subclass needs part of the base behavior but not all.
  • Your subclass would otherwise add new preconditions or side effects.
  • You want cleaner testing and decoupling of concerns.
Concrete example
Instead of EmailLogger inheriting Logger and adding email responsibilities, EmailLogger should hold a Logger instance and an EmailSender and delegate logging calls. This preserves Logger’s contract and keeps email behavior orthogonal.
Practical checklist
If a subclass must override many methods to no-op or throw, composition is a stronger design. Favor composition to reduce accidental contract changes.

screens.title: Printable document refactor (Python example)
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a concrete refactor that appears in the chapter. The original Document class exposes a print_document method that some subclasses, such as an encrypted document, cannot implement cleanly without additional state or user interaction. That breaks substitutability because clients that call print_document on Document instances may encounter decryption prompts or errors. The refactor extracts a Printable abstraction with a get_printable_content method. Simple documents return their content directly. Secure documents perform lazy decryption and return printable content when requested. The client then depends on Printable and calls a routine that prints any Printable object. The practical benefit is the client code no longer needs to know about encryption at all. A common misconception is to hide decryption in print_document; that couples input and output and security concerns. Extracting the printable contract separates responsibilities, makes unit testing straightforward, and preserves LSP. Below you will see the code example illustrating the pattern. After reviewing, ask: where in your codebase do methods reach for extra state to satisfy a subtype? Printable document refactor (Python example) means extract behaviors into focused interfaces so clients depend on stable, testable contracts rather than concrete implementations.. In practical terms, refactor document to a printable contract so secure and simple documents coexist. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Printable Refactor
Printable document refactor
A concrete Python example that restores substitutability
Refactored types
  • Printable — interface with get_printable_content.
  • SimpleDocument — returns content directly.
  • SecureDocument — lazy-decrypts then returns printable content.
Client impact
print_any_document accepts any Printable; clients don't need to handle encryption logic or catch decryption errors.
Code (excerpt)
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class Printable(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def get_printable_content(self) -> str:
        pass

class SimpleDocument(Printable):
    def __init__(self, content):
        self._content = content

    def get_printable_content(self) -> str:
        return self._content

class SecureDocument(Printable):
    def __init__(self, encrypted_content, decryption_key):
        self._encrypted_content = encrypted_content
        self._decryption_key = decryption_key
        self._decrypted_content = None

    def _decrypt(self):
        if self._decrypted_content is None:
            print("Decrypting document...")
            self._decrypted_content = f"DECRYPTED: {self._encrypted_content}"
        return self._decrypted_content

    def get_printable_content(self) -> str:
        return self._decrypt()

def print_any_document(doc: Printable):
    print("--- Printing Job ---")
    print(doc.get_printable_content())
    print("--- End Print Job ---")
Key Takeaway

Design small, focused contracts and let clients depend on them; this preserves substitutability and decouples concerns like security and printing.

screens.title: ReportGenerator: a common LSP trap
screens.narratorSegment: The ReportGenerator example in the chapter is a practical exercise in identifying an LSP violation and designing a refactor. Initially, a single ReportGenerator base class defines generate_report(data), and two subclasses, PDFReportGenerator and ExcelReportGenerator, inherit from it. PDFReportGenerator handles complex nested objects well, while ExcelReportGenerator expects flat lists of dictionaries and may raise a TypeError on complex inputs. This is an LSP violation because the Excel generator imposes extra preconditions the base type did not promise. The correct refactor is to split the abstraction into TabularReportGenerator for Excel-like outputs and DocumentReportGenerator for PDF-style outputs, or to extract a shared interface that only contains methods both can satisfy. Another approach is to keep one base type but have Excel generation be a composed adapter that accepts only tabular data, leaving clients that need PDFs to use the PDF generator directly. A common misconception is to simply catch and ignore Excel failures at the client; doing so hides the design problem and encourages fragile code. The right choice is to change the type relationships so clients don't pass incompatible data to a generator that cannot fulfill the contract. After this refactor, process_reports should call only appropriate generator abstractions and no longer encounter unexpected TypeError exceptions.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › ReportGenerator Case
ReportGenerator: a common LSP trap
Why Excel and PDF behaviors sometimes can't share one base type
Problem
ExcelReportGenerator requires flat tabular data and may throw on complex objects. PDFReportGenerator accepts complex nested objects. Passing the same data to both can cause TypeError for Excel, which is an LSP violation.
Refactoring approaches
  • Split into TabularReportGenerator and DocumentReportGenerator abstractions.
  • Use adapters that transform complex data into tabular form when appropriate.
  • Have client code choose the proper generator interface based on data shape.
Practical exercise
Refactor the starter code so process_reports either filters generators by capability or uses separate client functions for tabular and document reports. That preserves substitutability for each abstraction.

screens.title: Refactoring steps for the reporting system
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on plan walks you through refactoring the reporting system so it obeys LSP. Step one: add a capability specifier — a small interface or marker method that declares what data a generator accepts, for example supports_tabular_data(). Step two: run tests replacing base instances with each subclass so you can see failures and collect failing cases. Step three: extract interfaces. Create a TabularReportGenerator interface with a generate_report_tabular method and a DocumentReportGenerator interface for document-oriented outputs. Refactoring steps for the reporting system
A reproducible five-step workflow
Step 1: Detect
Run cases that exercise each generator and log unexpected exceptions or type checks. Collect failing inputs.
Step 2: Extract
Create TabularReportGenerator and DocumentReportGenerator interfaces that express clear preconditions.

screens.title: Common mistakes and practical checks
screens.narratorSegment: When applying LSP fixes, developers sometimes introduce new problems. This screen lists common mistakes and short checks to avoid them. First mistake: extracting an interface but leaving client code dependent on the full base class. Check: update clients to rely only on the new interface. Second mistake: over-extracting tiny interfaces until the A P I is fragmented. Check: group related behaviors that make sense together and keep the A P I discoverable. Third mistake: using inheritance for code reuse rather than behavioral correctness. Check: if you’re copying methods into subclasses or making no-op overrides, prefer composition. Fourth mistake: hiding failures in client code by catching and ignoring exceptions from a subtype. Check: fix the type relationships instead of masking the symptom. Practical checks: run substitutability tests, assert preconditions and postconditions in unit tests, and remove instanceof logic from production code. A final useful habit is to write small examples demonstrating that replacing a base instance with each subtype leaves client behavior unchanged. That live test is the quickest indicator of regressions. Common mistakes and practical checks
Short checklist to keep refactors safe
Mistake: Keeping clients on the old API
After extracting an interface, update clients so they no longer depend on the broad base class.

Balance specificity and discoverability; group related operations sensibly.

screens.narratorSegment: These are the essential ideas to carry forward: first, LSP violations appear as thrown exceptions, no-op overrides, or client-side type checks. Second, refactoring strategies that restore substitutability include extracting narrower interfaces and using composition rather than forcing an inheritance relationship. Third, design contracts explicitly by defining preconditions, postconditions, and invariants for methods so subclasses cannot narrow behavior unexpectedly. Keep these three points in mind when you inspect or evolve a codebase: detect the symptom, choose the smallest interface that expresses required behavior, and prefer delegation where semantic mismatch exists. What to Remember
Three final practical reminders to apply immediately

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how to spot real Liskov Substitution Principle violations in working code, and how to refactor them so clients never need to distinguish concrete subtypes. We’ll move from concrete indicators — methods that throw or silently do nothing — to practical fixes like extracting narrower interfaces and preferring composition. You will see real examples such as discount calculators, printable documents, and report generators. For each example we will name the violating behavior, show a refactoring pattern, and explain why the refactor restores substitutability. This matters because breaking LSP produces brittle code: client code begins to branch on types, to check instances, or to catch unexpected exceptions. Those symptoms hide design debt and increase maintenance cost. By following the checks and refactor patterns you’ll be able to design class hierarchies that are predictable, easier to test, and safer to extend. Think about the last time you saw an instanceof check in production: by the end of this chapter you’ll be able to ask the right questions and suggest a concrete refactor.

By the end of this chapter you will analyze existing code and detect LSP violations that show up as runtime surprises or client-side branching. You will practice concrete refactorings such as extracting narrower interfaces, introducing new abstractions, and applying composition to avoid behavioral mismatch. You will learn to weigh trade-offs encountered during real-world refactors, such as added indirection versus clearer contracts, and you will design new class hierarchies that preserve substitutability from the start. These skills matter because they reduce debugging time, avoid fragile client code, and improve testability and extensibility. For example, after learning the extract-interface technique you will be able to replace a single base class method that cannot be implemented by all subtypes with two smaller interfaces, enabling clients to depend only on the behavior they need. Think of these objectives as a practical checklist: identify, refactor, evaluate, and design. Each objective pairs a practical skill with why it matters in production systems.

These objectives extend into evaluating trade-offs and designing for LSP from the start. You will learn to weigh additional abstractions against complexity: extracting interfaces reduces surprising behavior but adds types to manage; composition reduces incorrect inheritance but can introduce indirection. We will practice concrete decision rules: when a method cannot be sensibly implemented by every subtype, prefer extracting a new interface or moving the behavior off the base class. You will also be asked to demonstrate a refactor in a small reporting system — converting a single base report generator into two clearer abstractions so PDF and Excel generators do not break each other’s contracts. Finally, you will design a short hierarchy and justify how preconditions, postconditions, and invariants are preserved. These skills let you prevent brittle code patterns like runtime type checks and unexpected exceptions and make code easier to test and safer to extend.

An LSP violation happens when a subtype cannot stand in for its base type without surprising clients. In practice this shows up as a handful of clear symptoms. One is methods that throw specific exceptions when a client expects general behavior. Another is methods that silently do nothing — for example a subclass that overrides a base method with an empty implementation; clients then receive no effect where one was expected. A third symptom is client code that performs type checks or branches based on subclass type instead of relying on polymorphism. Those branches are a sign the subclass does not preserve the base contract. Consider a logging class: if a subclass requires extra initialization and throws if it’s not provided, client calls that assume a simple log call will break. A misconception is to think that different return values alone imply violation — different results are acceptable if they still meet the base method’s postconditions. To be an LSP violation we need changed preconditions (the subtype requires more), changed postconditions (the subtype fails to meet promised results), or unexpected side effects. Example: a discount calculator that throws when not a first-time customer changes the precondition. The takeaway is simple: when a client must reason about concrete types or handle unexpected exceptions from an override, the design needs a narrower abstraction or a different composition. How might you test for substitutability in your codebase?

Understanding the difference between acceptable behavioral difference and an LSP violation is central to good design. A valid subtype can return different concrete values as long as it honors the base contract. For instance, two discount calculators that both return a numeric discount are substitutable even if the formulas differ. Contrast this with a subtype that returns zero for most inputs or throws when certain conditions are not met: that alters the expected postcondition or adds a new precondition. A helpful concrete example contrasts a StandardDiscountCalculator and a FirstTimeCustomerDiscountCalculator. The standard implementation applies a percent to the total and always returns a numeric discount. The first-time implementation, if written to throw for repeat customers, changes the contract and violates LSP. A misconception is to treat any conditional logic inside a subtype as a violation. Conditional behavior is fine if the method still meets all preconditions and postconditions the base type promises. The practical test is simple: can client code call the base method on the subtype in the same way and expect the same kinds of results and side effects? If not, refactor by splitting the abstraction or using composition. Which refactor will preserve behavior without adding client complexity?

A primary refactor for LSP problems is to extract a narrower abstraction that captures the true contract. When the base class exposes methods not meaningful for every subtype, the base is too broad. The fix is to split responsibilities: define smaller interfaces or abstract classes describing the capability precisely. For example, instead of a generic Vehicle that includes a refuel method, create a Refuelable interface. Car implements Refuelable, Bicycle does not. Client code that needs to refuel depends on Refuelable, not Vehicle. This prevents Bicycle being passed where refueling is expected. In practice perform the refactor in three steps: first, identify methods that cause violations; second, extract an interface with those methods and update types; third, migrate subclasses to implement the new interface only if they satisfy the contract. A common pitfall is extracting too many tiny interfaces without clear purpose; balance specificity and usability. Concrete scenario: the Document class with a print method that SecureDocument cannot implement without extra state. Extract a Printable interface with get_printable_content and have both simple and secure documents implement it. The client then prints any Printable without caring about encryption. Ask yourself: which methods in my base class are actually optional for some subclasses?

Composition is the alternative when a class needs certain behavior but does not truly 'is-a' the base type. Instead of inheriting and being forced to implement or disable methods, the class can hold an instance that provides the required functionality and delegate to it. That avoids adding preconditions or surprising side effects. A concrete example is a Logger that has FileLogger and DatabaseLogger as subclasses. If you then create an EmailLogger that primarily sends email but also logs, composition is a natural fit: EmailLogger should contain a Logger and an EmailSender rather than inherit from Logger and extend its responsibilities. This keeps Logger's contract intact and lets EmailLogger delegate only the parts it needs. A misconception is believing composition always adds more code; while it can introduce small forwarding methods, it preserves behavior and reduces the chance of violating contracts. Composition also makes testing simpler: you can inject a mock component rather than stub an inherited method. Ask yourself: does my subclass change the meaning of a base method? If yes, consider composition and delegation instead of inheritance. Use composition when 'is-a' fails means when behavior doesn't semantically match an 'is-a' relationship, prefer 'has-a' with delegation to preserve contracts and simplify testing.. In practical terms, delegate behavior instead of forcing incorrect inheritance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through a concrete refactor that appears in the chapter. The original Document class exposes a print_document method that some subclasses, such as an encrypted document, cannot implement cleanly without additional state or user interaction. That breaks substitutability because clients that call print_document on Document instances may encounter decryption prompts or errors. The refactor extracts a Printable abstraction with a get_printable_content method. Simple documents return their content directly. Secure documents perform lazy decryption and return printable content when requested. The client then depends on Printable and calls a routine that prints any Printable object. The practical benefit is the client code no longer needs to know about encryption at all. A common misconception is to hide decryption in print_document; that couples input and output and security concerns. Extracting the printable contract separates responsibilities, makes unit testing straightforward, and preserves LSP. Below you will see the code example illustrating the pattern. The ReportGenerator example in the chapter is a practical exercise in identifying an LSP violation and designing a refactor. Initially, a single ReportGenerator base class defines generate_report(data), and two subclasses, PDFReportGenerator and ExcelReportGenerator, inherit from it. PDFReportGenerator handles complex nested objects well, while ExcelReportGenerator expects flat lists of dictionaries and may raise a TypeError on complex inputs. This is an LSP violation because the Excel generator imposes extra preconditions the base type did not promise. The correct refactor is to split the abstraction into TabularReportGenerator for Excel-like outputs and DocumentReportGenerator for PDF-style outputs, or to extract a shared interface that only contains methods both can satisfy. Another approach is to keep one base type but have Excel generation be a composed adapter that accepts only tabular data, leaving clients that need PDFs to use the PDF generator directly. A common misconception is to simply catch and ignore Excel failures at the client; doing so hides the design problem and encourages fragile code. The right choice is to change the type relationships so clients don't pass incompatible data to a generator that cannot fulfill the contract. After this refactor, process_reports should call only appropriate generator abstractions and no longer encounter unexpected TypeError exceptions.
